text: Joseph Christian Leyendecker (March 23, 1874 – July 25, 1951) was one of the most prominent and financially successful freelance commercial artists in the United States, active from 1895 to 1951 and producing drawings and paintings for hundreds of posters, books, advertisements, and magazine covers and stories. He is best known for his 80 covers for Collier's Weekly, 322 covers for The Saturday Evening Post, and advertising illustrations for B. Kuppenheimer men's clothing and Arrow brand shirts and detachable collars. He was one of the few known reportedly gay artists working in the early-twentieth century United States. Born on March 23, 1874, in Montabaur, Germany, to Peter Leyendecker (1838–1916) and Elizabeth Ortseifen Leyendecker (1845–1905), he had a brother, Francis Xavier (aka "Frank"), born two years later. In 1882, the entire family immigrated to Chicago, Illinois, where Elizabeth's brother Adam Ortseifen was vice-president of the McAvoy Brewing Company; a sister, Augusta Mary, joined the family after their arrival. Leyendecker was of Sephardic Jewish ancestry through his father. As a teenager around 1890, he apprenticed at J. Manz & Company in Chicago, eventually becoming a staff artist and taking night classes at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. After studying drawing and anatomy under John Vanderpoel, he and Frank enrolled at the Académie Julian in Paris from October 1895 through June 1897. Upon returning to Chicago, they took an apartment in Hyde Park and shared a studio at 410 South Michigan Ave. While in Paris, Leyendecker continued working for Hart, Schaffner & Marx, produced 12 covers for The Inland Printer, and won a contest (out of 700 entries) for the midsummer 1896 issue of The Century Magazine, which received national coverage. He also won four awards at the Académie Julian and had his painting "Portrait of My Brother" exhibited in the Paris salon in 1897. One of his posters for Hart, Schaffner & Marx, titled "The Horse Show," was included in the award-winning display of American manufacturers' posters at the Exposition Universelle (1900) in Paris. After returning in June 1897, he illustrated for local clients including Hart, Schaffner & Marx, Carson, Pirie & Scott, the Eastern Illinois Railroad, the Northern Pacific Railroad, Woman's Home Companion, The Osprey, and books such as Conan Doyle's Micah Clarke and Octave Thanet's A Book of True Lovers. He also painted 132 scenes of America for L. W. Yaggy's Royal Scroll, a Bible-themed panorama published by Powers, Fowler & Lewis. On May 20, 1899, he received his first commission for a cover of The Saturday Evening Post, beginning a forty-four-year association with the magazine that eventually included 322 covers, introducing iconic images such as the New Year's Baby, the pudgy red-garbed Santa Claus, flowers for Mother's Day, and firecrackers on the 4th of July. During the 1890s, he exhibited with and attended events at the Palette and Chisel Club, the Art Students League, and the Chicago Society of Artists; his posters were shown at Siegel, Cooper & Company in December 1895 and at Kimball Cafetier in January 1898. After moving to New York City in 1902, he worked for a wide range of increasingly prominent clients, including A. B. Kirschbaum, Wick Fancy Hat Bands, Gillette Safety Razors, E. Howard & Co. watches, Ivory Soap, Williams Shaving Cream, Karo Corn Syrup, Kingsford's Corn Starch, Interwoven socks, B. Kuppenheimer & Co., Cooper Underwear, and Cluett Peabody & Company, maker of Arrow brand shirts and detachable collars and cuffs. The male models in his 1907–30 Arrow shirt and collar ads were often called "the" Arrow Collar Man, though multiple men served as models, some of whom achieved success in theater, film, and television, including Brian Donlevy, Fredric March, Jack Mulhall, Neil Hamilton, Ralph Forbes, and Reed Howes. Charles A. Beach (1881–1954), a Canadian-born model, began working with Leyendecker in 1903 and appeared in many of his illustrations. The two maintained a nearly 50-year professional and personal relationship, which many biographers describe as romantic and sexual. Leyendecker never married and lived with Beach from 1903 until his death in 1951; Beach served as his studio manager and frequent model. In 1915, J. C., Frank, and Augusta Mary moved to a newly built home and art studio in New Rochelle, New York. After 1918, Beach also moved into the home. The couple hosted large galas that were significant social and celebrity events. Beach organized many of these gatherings and, according to Norman Rockwell, contributed to Leyendecker's social isolation in his later years by forbidding outside contact. Leyendecker enjoyed a luxurious lifestyle with a large home, domestic servants, and a chauffeured car, but during the Great Depression, commissions declined, forcing him to cut back on spending. By the time of his death, he had dismissed all household staff and lived with Beach at their New Rochelle estate. He died on July 25, 1951, from an acute coronary occlusion at his home in New Rochelle and was buried alongside his parents and brother Frank at Woodlawn Cemetery in The Bronx. His will divided his estate—house, furnishings, paintings, etc.—equally between his sister Augusta Mary and Charles Beach. Although he instructed Beach to burn his drawings upon his death, Beach sold many at a lawn sale. Other works were sold through the Society of Illustrators or donated to the New York Public Library and Metropolitan Museum of Art. Augusta Mary retained many paintings, which she later donated to the Haggin Museum upon her death. The largest public collection of Leyendecker's original works is at the Haggin Museum in Stockton, California, where the Leyendecker Gallery displays over 40 pieces and personal ephemera. Original works are also held at the Metropolitan Museum of Art (New York City), Norman Rockwell Museum (Stockbridge, MA), National Museum of American Illustration (Newport, RI), Lucas Museum of Narrative Art (Los Angeles, CA), and the Pritzker Military Museum & Library (Chicago, IL). Reproductions are found in major archives and libraries, including the Hagley Museum and Library (Wilmington, DE), Winterthur Museum, Garden and Library (Wilmington, DE), New York Public Library (New York, NY), and the D. B. Dowd Modern Graphic History Library Archives at Washington University in St. Louis (St. Louis, MO). As the premier cover illustrator for The Saturday Evening Post for much of the first half of the 20th century, Leyendecker helped shape American visual culture, popularizing the image of Santa Claus as a jolly fat man in a red fur-trimmed coat and the New Year's Baby. His May 30, 1914, cover depicting a young bellhop carrying hyacinths introduced the tradition of giving flowers on Mother's Day, commemorating President Woodrow Wilson's declaration of the holiday. He was a major influence and friend of Norman Rockwell, who was a pallbearer at Leyendecker's funeral; Rockwell's early work for the Post bears strong resemblance to Leyendecker's, with many of Rockwell's iconic images being derivative or reinterpretations of Leyendecker's themes. Leyendecker's visual style inspired the graphics in The Dagger of Amon Ra video game and designs in Team Fortress 2. George Lucas has acknowledged Leyendecker's influence and his work will be part of the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art collection. His 1914 cover "Beat-up Boy, Football Hero" sold for $4.12 million on May 7, 2021, and his 1930 work "Carousel Ride" sold for $516,100 in December 2020. Costume designer Carol Cutshall drew inspiration from Leyendecker's illustrations for the male characters Louis de Pointe du Lac and Lestat de Lioncourt in the 2022 AMC series Interview with the Vampire, noting that their formalwear and tuxedos directly reflect Leyendecker's art and drawing a parallel between the characters' hidden romantic relationship and Leyendecker's relationship with Beach. The play Love with the Arrow Collar Man, written by Lance Ringel and directed by Chuck Muckle at Theatre 80 St. Marks from November to December 2017, dramatizes Leyendecker's life and his relationship with Beach. The 2021 documentary Coded tells the story of Leyendecker and premiered at the TriBeCa Film Festival.
